item.title: A Metamaterial Agentic Swarm: Coordinated Search for Discrete Mechanical Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.26743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing discrete metamaterial assemblies is challenging because local unit-cell choices collectively determine the global elastic response. We present Metamaterial Agentic Swarm, an island-based portfolio of forty specialized numerical search agents for unit-cell selection in a pixel-resolved mechanical cloak. Five cooperating islands each contain eight agents responsible for global sampling, spatial proposals, mutation, learning, recombination, diversity, neighborhood exploration, and polishing. Islands maintain separate parents while exchanging evaluated assignments through an elite archive and recombination. The objective is the relative exterior displacement mismatch on a supplied observation mask. Candidate designs are scored by the mismatch in exterior displacement, computed with a symmetry-reduced finite-element model at full pixel resolution. Starting from random assignments within the supplied candidate libraries, the swarm achieves final displacement losses of 0.100590, 0.139274, and 0.135858 at a retrospectively selected reporting endpoint of 961 charged queries per run. Seed 0 achieved the lowest swarm loss, L=0.100590, which is 8.72% below the comparison threshold of 0.1102; the other two runs did not reach this threshold. While they do not establish comparative efficiency or causal benefits from coordination, the results represent a first step towards using agentic swarms for large discrete assembly problems.
item.dc:creator: Achuth Chandrasekhar, Alexander Zhao, Amir Barati Farimani

item.title: InfantConnect: integrating developmental brain atlases and electrophysiological network analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.26911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The brains of infants change considerably during the first two years. Hence, developmental neuroimaging requires computational tools that account for age-related anatomy while supporting the analysis of electrophysiological data. For instance, cortical surfaces, electrode montages, tractography atlases, and electroencephalography (EEG) analysis utilities are commonly distributed across separate resources and software environments. Here we propose an open Python framework that brings these components into a shared three-dimensional workspace and supplements interactive visualization with command-line tools for EEG quality control, preprocessing, source-related visualization, and effective-connectivity analysis. The command line version can also be invoked by a model context protocol server to be used by artificial intelligence agents. The tool supports age-indexed cortical surfaces, infant scalp and skull templates, electrode locations, tractography, sensor-level connectomes, and directed estimates based on Granger causality and transfer entropy. We demonstrate the resource using representative anatomical visualizations and evaluate the effective-connectivity workflow on controlled toy networks with explicitly specified nodes and directed interactions. These tests provide targeted evidence about the connectivity workflow rather than a general validation of causal inference from clinical EEG. Performance benchmarks on low resolution electromagnetic tomography and validation of effective connectivity are provided.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Crimi, Pawe{\l} Grybo\'s

item.title: Data-Driven Detection of Volatility Regimes and Sector-Level Asymmetry During Sovereign Default
item.description: arXiv:2611.26967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a data-driven framework for detecting changes in stock-market volatility and characterising their effects across industry sectors. The framework identifies volatility regimes directly from historical returns using dynamic programming, validated with a sup-F test and a Markov-switching model. We apply it to 1,559 trading days of the Sri Lankan All Share Price Index (ASPI) and 13 sector indices, covering pre-COVID, COVID-19, sovereign-default, and recovery periods. Within each regime, Student-$t$ EGARCH models quantify volatility response, persistence, and asymmetry between positive and negative shocks. The results reveal a distinct regime-specific pattern: significant negative-shock asymmetry occurs in 9 of 14 series during the sovereign default, compared with none during COVID-19 despite 2.6 times higher volatility than pre-COVID. For the ASPI, volatility persistence decreases from 0.936 during COVID-19 to 0.647 during the default. Cross-sector correlations increase during the default but largely disappear after adjusting for increased variance, providing little evidence of stronger shock propagation. Macroeconomic variables explain less than 4% of ASPI forecast-error variance at a 30-day horizon. These findings demonstrate how combining automated regime detection with interpretable time-series models can uncover structural changes hidden by aggregate analysis.
item.dc:creator: M. J. S. Ahamed, M. R. Hatheem, M. A. H. Ahamed, U. I. Jayasekara, H. Y. Ahamed, Madara Mendis, Nevidu Jayatilleke, Nisansa de Silva, Sandareka Wickramanayake

item.title: Spatiotemporal Landslide Runout Reconstruction from Sparse Observations with LAPIS-SHRED
item.description: arXiv:2611.27132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of landslide runout from limited observations is a central challenge in geohazard assessment: transient flow dynamics are rarely observed directly, and available data are often confined to post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. We apply LAPIS-SHRED (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders) to reconstruct runout events near Mount St. Helens, USA. Trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, the framework supports both backward reconstruction from single frame and forward prediction from short initial window across different runout regimes. Using 32 sensor observations from a single timepoint, LAPIS-SHRED recovers complete runout trajectories with NRMSE below 5.8%, robust across varying observational and training conditions. Validation against observed deposits yields spatial correlation of r = 0.843 against the calibrated simulator's r = 0.853. These results suggest that latent-space temporal inference offers a viable pathway for spatiotemporal landslide reconstruction under extreme observational constraints typical of field settings.
item.dc:creator: Xingyue Zhang, Yuxuan Bao, Jeffrey Keck, Erkan Istanbulluoglu, J. Nathan Kutz

item.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization
item.description: arXiv:2611.27246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics is essential for comprehensive protein characterization, yet it relies on multistep computational workflows that typically demand tedious manual parameter tuning and complex software integration. Here, we present MSRyzen, an agent-driven framework that provides automated parameter optimization and extensible tool integration across bottom-up and top-down proteomics workflows. MSRyzen translates natural-language prompts into directed acyclic workflow graphs, optimizes analytical parameters guided by quantitative metrics and user-defined objectives, and incorporates new third-party software through standardized callable interfaces. Across four public top-down datasets, automated parameter optimization increased proteoform identifications by 3.6% to 15.8% compared to default settings at a 1% false discovery rate. To ensure transparent data interpretation, an interactive visualization interface coordinates identification metrics with peak-level spectral evidence and sequence coverage. Integrating adaptive tuning with multi-tiered spectral inspection, MSRyzen delivers an end-to-end, fully automated framework, dramatically reducing the operational barrier to modern mass spectrometry data analysis.
item.dc:creator: Yucheng Liao, Jubao Cheng, Zexu Xiao, Tao Yi, Jiaxiang Ding, Weijie Zhang

item.title: Gradient-based optimization of buoyancy distributions for lazy-wave risers
item.description: arXiv:2611.27361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a novel gradient-based approach for optimizing the buoyancy distribution of lazy-wave offshore risers. The static response is modeled with a total potential energy formulation for a geometrically nonlinear, inextensible beam on an elastic seabed. The total potential energy is discretized by finite differences and the resulting nonlinear equilibrium system is solved by a two stage continuation procedure, in which the line length and then the buoyancy load are increased incrementally, with Newton--Raphson iterations and an Armijo line search. The design variables are the uplift ratios at the nodes where buoyancy modules may be installed. The optimization minimizes a quadratic measure of buoyancy demand subject to constraints on the maximum curvature and effective tension. The gradients of the constraints are computed by means of a discrete adjoint sensitivity analysis. Three design parametrizations are compared: a continuous formulation with independent nodal uplift ratios, a grouped formulation with fixed module assignments, and a formulation inspired by discrete material optimization that simultaneously selects the uplift ratios of a small catalog of module types and their placement along the riser. The latter yields practical designs with a limited number of module sizes. The framework provides a flexible and computationally efficient tool for preliminary design of lazy-wave configurations.
item.dc:creator: Nicol\`o Pollini, Kazem Jaber

item.title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.27427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.
item.dc:creator: Mingxuan Wang, Siyuan Du, Yanfeng Wang, Ya Zhang, Chencheng Zhang, Jiangchao Yao

item.title: Gauge-equivariant real-space renormalization of frustrated magnets and topological spin textures
item.description: arXiv:2611.27598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-space renormalization group transformations and equilibrium Monte Carlo sampling are foundational tools of statistical physics, yet both break down in frustrated and chiral magnets. Fixed geometric coarse-graining blocks average anti-aligned sublattices and erase emergent gauge fluxes on triangular, ruby, spin-glass and multi-shell lattices, whereas local Monte Carlo dynamics suffer catastrophic topological freezing between distinct winding-number sectors below the skyrmion-ordering transition. Here we show that decimating non-adjacent spins while preserving local bond-rotation rules defines an exact-likelihood, gauge-equivariant real-space renormalization flow that overcomes both barriers simultaneously. Through exact matrix coarsening of the coupled spin network, the flow extracts a gauge-invariant frustration deficit measuring destructive loop interference, separating unfrustrated order, spin liquids and spin glasses while recovering exact Wannier residual entropy. Paired with an annealed sequence of parallel heat-bath and energy-conserving over-relaxation sweeps, the method matches thermodynamic integration to 0.01% on density-functional-calibrated fcc-Pd/Fe/Ir(111), maps its finite-temperature skyrmion melting boundary, images a 30% softening of domain-wall magnon stiffness in centrosymmetric Gd$_2$PdSi$_3$, and models experimental 219-atom ruby-lattice Rydberg spin-liquid snapshots, linking frustrated statistical mechanics to live spin-polarized quantum readout.
item.dc:creator: Musen Li, Tianhao Su, Shunbo Hu, Tong-Yi Zhang

item.title: Report2Alpha-Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents on End-to-End Quantitative Research
item.description: arXiv:2611.27635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate whether LLM agents can independently carry out a several-hour quantitative research project: read a brokerage research report, make a plan, and over 7 rounds of iteration propose hypotheses, write factor code and improve it from backtest feedback, seeing only 2022-2023 market data. Like Terminal-Bench-Science, the task evaluates overall research ability; unlike it, there is no directly checkable unique answer: the model must repeatedly propose hypotheses on very noisy data, revise its understanding from experiments, disentangle multiple factors and design ablations without overfitting in-sample, much like complex real-world decisions with many interacting factors. After the research, a fixed rule using only 2022-2023 results selects a low-correlated factor pool from all candidates the model produced, and scores it on unseen 2024-2025 data after removing common style returns such as size and momentum; the same rule on round-0 candidates alone gives a report baseline that "implements the report without iterating". We run gpt-6.1-sol (reasoning effort xhigh), gpt-6.1-terra (xhigh), muse-spark-1.3 (xhigh) and deepseek-v4.1-flash (max) once on each of 7 reports. Of the 28 runs, 19 factor pools pass the usability threshold; the average score is 48.4 (0-100 scale), against 25.4 for the report baseline and 35.9 for the models' own picks. From similar report baselines (17.0-31.0), the models separate after iteration to 74.7 (gpt-6.1-sol), 56.6 (gpt-6.1-terra), 35.8 (deepseek-v4.1-flash) and 26.2 (muse-spark-1.3); their candidates look equally good in training and diverge only in testing, with the leaders proposing more diverse ideas per round and ending with more effective factors in the pool. Evaluating research agents thus requires scoring on frozen future data after removing styles, and measuring "what the research produced" separately from "what was finally picked".
item.dc:creator: Yun Zhang, Hui Yang, Wei Meng

item.title: DOiT: Better Money-Flow Ranking Can Coexist with Worse Account Selection in Anti-Money Laundering Review
item.description: arXiv:2611.27809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) review selects suspicious accounts and reconstructs transfers. Downstream graph neural networks (GNNs) rank money-flow evidence but may also reorder the account queue. DOiT separates these decisions at equal review capacity: account selection determines where graph investigation starts. Across AMLWorld and AMLNet, GNN reordering harms higher-yield upstream orders but helps lower-yield ones. On AMLWorld, this harm coexists with higher transaction average precision (AP) in dimension-matched, per-run decoders, demonstrating separable ranking abilities. At small capacities, positive neighbors can displace a denser upstream prefix and lower yield; replacement costs fall as that prefix is exhausted, allowing the preferred order to reverse. A restricted-access synthetic benchmark informed by real transaction patterns reproduces this separation and validation-based upstream preservation. Capacity-matched combination protects upstream ordering while retaining GNN money-flow analysis, admitting GNN queue influence only where held-out evidence supports it.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026), pp. 819~826, 2026

item.title: How Much of a Calculation-Error Rate Is Not Arithmetic: Auditing the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 Metric with a Deterministic Rule System
item.description: arXiv:2611.27192v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic. The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Beskorovainyi

item.title: Critical slowing down in hive temperature does not provide actionable early warnings of honey bee colony collapse
item.description: arXiv:2611.27766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early warning signals (EWS) based on critical slowing down (CSD) have been proposed as model-independent indicators of approaching ecological regime shifts and may help anticipate honeybee colony collapse. However, whether theoretically expected signals can be reliably observed and provide useful prediction in real-world systems remains uncertain. Here, we combine structural analysis, mechanistic modeling and longitudinal observations to assess the dynamical plausibility, detectability and predictive accuracy of CSD-based EWS for honeybee colony collapse. Our results show that the presence of EWS is not equivalent to successful prediction of the transition. The analyzed models exhibit regime shifts accompanied by CSD, but detecting these signals in finite and noisy observations requires longer and more densely sampled time series than typically available for practical monitoring. Moreover, in empirical temperature records, CSD-like trends were detectable but provided limited discrimination between colonies that subsequently collapsed and those that survived. Declining mean temperature provided slightly greater discrimination than conventional CSD indicators, although its predictive value remained modest. Non-Gaussian correlated noise and the imperfect correspondence between hive temperature and colony strength further constrained EWS performance. These findings show that EWS can exist at the dynamical level without becoming useful predictors at the observational level, at least for our case study, thus cautioning against treating CSD-based indicators as generic predictors of ecological collapse.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Proverbio, Els Weinans, Davide Frizzera, Desiderato Annoscia, Francesco Nazzi, Giulia Giordano

item.title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph.
item.dc:creator: Samarth Sarin, Lovepreet Singh, Dhagash Mehta

item.title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
item.description: arXiv:2610.25898v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns in continuous recordings. Repeated template reconstruction and time-pair correlation scans make analyses across brain regions, large cohorts, and parameter sweeps computationally prohibitive. We present HP-GSBS, an open-source implementation built on an exact mathematical reformulation that decomposes the matching objective into additive interval contributions from temporal prefix sums and computes Welch t-distance through constant-time rectangle queries over two-dimensional correlation prefix tables. Combined with streaming candidate search, local-window refinement, and active-block caching, this formulation drives unified CPU, PyTorch CUDA, and Triton backends. Across controlled benchmarks spanning recording lengths, feature dimensions, and search depths, HP-GSBS achieves 154- to 1,730-fold speedups while identically reproducing reference boundary histories and selected state counts (maximum $|\Delta\mathrm{TD}|=1.88\times10^{-11}$). Cross-backend numerical equivalence is further confirmed on four human electroencephalography recordings from the Brain, Body, and Behavior Dataset (120--173 states). Applied to naturalistic movie-viewing functional magnetic resonance imaging from 16 participants (4,230 angular-gyrus voxels), HP-GSBS completes group and individual fits in 213.10 s on a single CPU and reveals intersubject boundary alignment above a circular-shift null (mean pairwise $F_1=0.414$ vs. 0.325, $p=0.001$). HP-GSBS reduces hour-scale benchmark fits to seconds or fractions of a second. Recording-level parallelism and an optional low-memory execution path make cohort-level and multi-timescale analyses tractable on standard laboratory hardware.
item.dc:creator: Yanzhe Zhao, Yongzhang Ji

item.title: AutoDFT: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous DFT Calculations
item.description: arXiv:2605.26179v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) serves as the basis for computational discovery in materials science and chemistry, yet each calculation demands extensive human effort: adjusting algorithms when convergence stalls, revising plans when unexpected physics emerges, and inserting steps as intermediate results reshape the problem. Existing LLM-based agents automate only the initial planning stage, producing a full execution plan upfront and leaving all subsequent adaptation to hand-crafted rules. As a result, these workflows remain fragile, do not generalize well beyond pre-planned scenarios, and often require expert intervention when failures or unexpected intermediate results require changes to the calculation path. Here, we introduce AutoDFT, a closed-loop multi-agent framework that embeds LLM reasoning into every stage of the DFT lifecycle, where a strategic planner produces a skeletal plan of step objectives; a step planner generates numerical parameters just in time from preceding results; and a monitor-recover-reflect cycle diagnoses failures, repairs them, and revises the plan when the evidence justifies it. We demonstrate both breadth and depth: breadth on VASPBench, a purpose-built benchmark spanning 34 tasks and 9 DFT calculation types, where AutoDFT achieves 94.1% task-level success with GPT-5.2; and depth on established materials databases, where AutoDFT produces quantitatively reliable property predictions across electronic, magnetic, and energetic properties. By closing the loop between planning and execution, AutoDFT enables experimentalists without deep computational expertise to obtain reliable first-principles results. Our code is available at https://github.com/penghui-yang/AutoDFT.
item.dc:creator: Penghui Yang, Zhonghan Zhang, Yue Li, Xinrun Wang, Yanchen Deng, Yuhao Lu, Bijun Tang, Zheng Liu, Bo An

item.title: A unified perspective of Gaussian process approximation for differential equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.06292v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The use of Gaussian processes for approximating differential equations has expanded rapidly, leading to a growing, diverse, and fragmented body of numerical methods. We present a unified Bayesian perspective that places these techniques within a common probabilistic framework, based on a derivative matching interpretation for incorporating differential equation constraints into likelihood. This unified perspective supports both parameter estimation and solution approximation, and shows how a range of existing methods can be understood within it. This work aims to consolidate current developments and provide a foundation for future research.
item.dc:creator: Mengwu Guo
